newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM surprises by calling fresh elections.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM surprises by calling fresh elections.

text.p: Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa on Friday dissolved parliament and called fresh elections on November 17, a move that surprised many members of the public and angered some key coalition partners.
Banharn had been widely expected to quit this Saturday, as promised last weekend, after picking someone to replace him.

But the wily premier, who kept the nation and his allies guessing for nearly a week over his next move, finally flashed his trump card on allies who had humiliated him and forced him to declare his resignation.
He had earlier conveyed his decision to hold fresh polls at a failed meeting of the 14-month-old, six-party coalition's leaders.
Banharn then went on television, soon after a royal proclamation for the dissolution was made, to explain the reasons for his decision.
"The process of selecting my successor could not take place smoothly. And it is generally believed that a multi-party coalition government could lead to conflicts and political problems...," he said.
"And it is generally believed that a multi-party coalition government could lead to conflicts and political problems," he added.
"I therefore see it appropriate to dissolve the house so as to return the important mandate of political determination to the people at this turning point," he added.
Banharn vowed to be an honest caretaker prime minister and said he would supervise a new election fairly.

The premier had agreed to quit last Saturday in return for support from his allies at a no-confidence vote against him in parliament. Banharn later won the vote with their support, but he was embarrassed and effectively lost hold of his job.
Coalition leaders had been meeting frequently since last Saturday to try to find a replacement for Banharn.
Banharn avoided their meetings and kept them in suspense. Earlier in the week, he met King Bhumibol Adulyadej but declined to say what had transpired at the audience.
Political sources believe he might have already informed the monarch then that he wanted to dissolve the house, but kept the matter secret from his partners.

Many politicians and analysts were surprised by Banharn's move because they had expected his Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, leader of the New Aspiration Party (NAP) that is the second largest in the coalition, to succeed him.

But Banharn's supporters in his Chart Thai party, which controlled 91 of the 209 coalition seats in the 391-seat parliament, refused to support the ambitious Chavalit. They saw him as the man who engineered the premier's downfall.
There was no immediate comment from Chavalit.

A Chavalit ally, Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan, who is also in charge of economic affairs in the administration, said: "It (the decision) surprised me because he had promised that he would not dissolve the house."
Another Chavalit ally, Justice Minister Chalerm Yoobamrung, who heads the small Muon Chon party, demanded an explanation from Banharn.

Members of the business community, hit recently by a slowing economy and weak stock market, welcomed the dissolution, which was an option they had believed would overcome the past week's political stalemate.
"Psychologically, this is important, at least there is an end to this uncertainty," said Janjai Tulayasathien, managing director of Chao Phraya Finance and Securities.
